title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Kansas City, MO: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Kansas City: vendor surveillance, rail, auto plants, bridges and pipelines, plus Part B site choices. Request a quote today.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Kansas City: Six Days of Preparation for Inspectors on Both Sides of the State Line
html:
Kansas City straddles a state line, and so does its welding work. A fabricator in North Kansas City may ship girders to a Kansas bridge, an inspector living in Olathe may spend the week at a plant in Missouri, and a design firm downtown may send someone to a vendor shop three states away to check welds before equipment leaves the floor. Across all of that, the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential is the qualification employers and specifications name most often. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day (6-day) CWI exam-preparation course for welders, fitters, QC technicians, NDT technicians and engineers on both sides of the line: study it online at your own pace, or have the six days delivered at your employer's facility for a group. AWS is the body that decides eligibility, runs the examination and grants the certification; Atlantis simply gets you ready for it. For pricing, send a Kansas City enquiry.

One metro, two states, two sets of public owners

The metro's split between Missouri and Kansas matters to a welding inspector in practical ways. Highway bridges on the Missouri side belong to the Missouri Department of Transportation or local agencies, and those on the Kansas side to the Kansas Department of Transportation or theirs, each with its own fabricator requirements, contract specifications and inspection staff. Building permits are issued city by city, and while most jurisdictions here base their codes on the International Building Code, the edition and local amendments vary. A CWI working the whole metro learns to read the project specification first and assume nothing from the last job across the line.

The workforce moves freely, which is good for candidates. Experience gained in either state counts the same for AWS, and the credential is national, so a Kansas City CWI is not tied to one state's agencies. That portability is one reason the CWI is so widely held here compared with narrower, owner-specific qualifications.

Owner's engineers and vendor surveillance

Kansas City is home to several large engineering, procurement and construction firms that design power plants, transmission and substation structures, water and wastewater plants, pipelines and industrial facilities across the country. Those firms, and the owners they work for, need inspectors who can visit a fabricator's shop, review its welding procedures and welder qualifications, watch critical welds, check dimensions and visual quality, and release equipment for shipment. That work is often called source inspection or vendor surveillance, and a CWI is the usual minimum qualification for the welding portion of it.

Source inspection rewards a particular set of skills. You arrive at a shop you may never have seen, with a purchase order, drawings and a specification that may cite several codes at once. You have to find the governing acceptance criteria fast, decide whether a procedure covers the work on the floor, and write findings the vendor cannot misread. That is close to what Part C of the CWI exam tests: working in an unfamiliar code book under time pressure. Understanding how procedures and welder tests fit together is the core of the job; the WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer is a good primer. If vendor work leads you toward API inspector roles, note those are separate credentials, compared in CWI versus API 577 versus ASNT Level II; Atlantis does not prepare candidates for API exams.

Vehicle assembly and the supplier base

The metro has vehicle assembly plants on both sides of the state line and a supplier network around them stamping, welding and assembling frames, brackets, seat structures and body components. Most of that welding is resistance spot welding and robotic gas metal arc welding, inspected to the automaker's own standards. Plant welding inspectors spend their days on teardown and chisel checks of spot welds, macro-etch sections of arc welds, robot program verification after changeovers, and statistical tracking of defects by cell.

Automotive standards are not on the AWS Part C list, but they share the language and logic of the AWS codes. A supplier inspector who masters welding symbols, discontinuities and destructive testing for Part A, and D1.1 for Part C, carries that discipline straight into a customer audit. For the NDT side of automotive quality, see magnetic particle testing in automotive manufacturing.

Rail yards and railcar repair

Kansas City has been one of the country's main rail junctions for well over a century, with large classification yards, intermodal terminals and repair shops for freight cars and locomotives. Railcar repair involves welding on car bodies, underframes, couplers and tank car components under railroad industry rules and, for tank cars, federal hazardous materials regulations. Fatigue is the dominant concern: welds at the toes of attachments and in highly stressed areas crack under cyclic load, and an inspector who understands weld profile, undercut and stress concentration catches problems that a quick look misses.

Rail repair shops do not usually need a CWI by rule, but they value one for quality leadership, procedure control and customer audits, and the credential opens doors if a repair welder later moves into structural or pipeline inspection. Rail parts are frequently examined further after a visual check; see ultrasonic testing in rail for what follows.

Grain, farm equipment and food plants

Kansas City grew as a grain and livestock market, and agriculture still shapes its industry. Grain elevators, steel bins, conveyors and bucket elevators are welded structures that are built and repaired constantly across Kansas and Missouri. Farm and construction equipment makers in the region weld frames, booms and implements, and food and animal health manufacturers install stainless process lines. Each brings its own inspection emphasis: structural integrity and fatigue for elevators and equipment, sanitary weld quality for food plants.

Code choice follows the work. Equipment and storage structures usually point to AWS D1.1; stainless process piping points to ASME B31.3; and if your employer works with thin sheet steel for bins and enclosures, AWS D1.3 governs sheet steel, although it is not among the Part C books AWS currently lists, so you would still choose D1.1 or another listed code for the exam. Check the current list on aws.org when you apply.

Bridges over the Missouri and Kansas rivers

Two rivers meet in Kansas City, and highways cross both on long steel and concrete bridges, with many more structures on the interstates radiating from the metro. Bridge rehabilitation and replacement keep steel fabricators and inspection consultants busy for both state departments of transportation. Girders and other primary highway bridge members follow AWS D1.5; candidates may bring its 2020 edition, fracture-critical provisions included, to Part C. Candidates at bridge fabricators or consultants should prepare with D1.5; the D1.5 summary outlines what sets it apart from the building code, and ultrasonic weld inspection covers the volumetric testing bridge groove welds usually receive.

Warehouses, data centers and special inspection

Interstate access has made the metro a distribution center, and recent years have added large data center and manufacturing construction projects. These are steel-framed buildings with long-span roofs, heavy equipment platforms and large volumes of field welding. Under building codes based on the International Building Code, structural steel welding on many such projects requires special inspection by an agency the owner engages, and the people that agency puts on the steel are usually CWIs, whose reports go to the structural engineer and the permitting authority. For these candidates, AWS D1.1 is the standard Part C choice; the D1.1 overview explains its structure.

Pipelines across the Plains

Crude oil, refined products and natural gas pipelines cross Kansas and Missouri, and construction, replacement and integrity projects on those lines need welding inspectors on the right-of-way. Pipeline girth welds are made and accepted under API 1104, available for Part C in its 22nd edition. A Kansas City candidate who expects to work pipeline spreads should prepare with that standard; see the API 1104 summary and ultrasonic testing on pipelines for the testing that follows the welders.

Choosing a Part B site from Kansas City

Two of the three exam parts can be taken locally. Fundamentals, with its 150 questions, and the open-book code paper, with 50 to 65, both run on a computer at Prometric's supervised centers once AWS has accepted your application. Part B, the Practical (46 questions tied to hands-on tasks using equipment AWS supplies), is held solely where AWS runs seminars, on dates AWS fixes, and the November 2026 AWS list has no site in Kansas City or elsewhere in Missouri or Kansas.

When choosing where to sit Part B, weigh these points:

  • Distance: Tulsa is the closest listed site for most of the metro; Dallas, Denver, Chicago and Indianapolis are further options.
  • Dates: applications for a US practical close roughly a month and a half ahead of it, so choose the exam day first and count backward.
  • Travel: AWS advises waiting for the confirmation letter before booking. Plan to arrive the day before rather than driving in on exam morning.
  • Scoring: each part needs at least 72 percent on its own, so a strong Part A will not rescue a weak practical.

Pages for nearby markets: CWI exam prep in Tulsa, CWI exam prep in St. Louis and CWI exam prep in Denver. For a sense of where candidates lose marks, read the Part A, B and C breakdown.

Welding colleges and the AWS Kansas City Section

Both sides of the metro have public welding programs. Johnson County Community College in Overland Park offers a Welding Technology/Metal Fabrication program whose certificate prepares students for the AWS D1.1 structural welding certification, and the program holds AWS SENSE accreditation. Metropolitan Community College in Kansas City, Missouri, also lists a welding technology program. Coursework like this counts toward AWS eligibility, reducing the years of experience required, so keep your records.

The American Welding Society's Kansas City Section, in District 16, is the local chapter for the metro; AWS lists a separate Kansas Section in the same district. Section meetings are where local CWIs, fabricators and instructors meet, and they are useful for finding a study partner, comparing notes on Part B sites, and meeting the supervisors who can verify your experience.

Fitting six days into a Kansas City schedule

The course works through six blocks in order. Block one covers welding processes, AWS terms, joints and the reading of welding symbols. Block two adds metallurgy, mechanical tests, discontinuities and what causes them, NDT methods, safety and what an inspector is responsible for. Block three is practical readiness for Part B: handling gauges, sizing welds, judging profile and applying a written specification. Block four is spent inside your chosen code book. Block five is timed practice papers across all three parts, and block six goes back to whatever those papers exposed, with exam logistics and an application checklist at the end. The national AWS CWI preparation page describes each block in full.

Online, you receive the plan, the reading, original practice questions and access to an instructor for questions by message, and you control the pace, which suits inspectors who travel for vendor work. For an employer, the six days can run at your plant, shop or yard for a group, and the practical block uses your gauges and your own production or repair welds. Atlantis has its offices in Houston and Hyderabad and none in Kansas City, so for on-site delivery the instructor travels to you. No practice question is lifted from an AWS paper; each is written new against the published topics. For extra practice judging weld surfaces, try the welding workshop simulator.

Eligibility at a glance

AWS weighs schooling against years of welding-related work. In summary:

Highest educationYears of experience AWS asks for
Welding engineering or welding technology bachelor'sOne
Relevant associate degree (engineering, engineering technology or physical science)Two
College engineering or technical classes that would apply to a welding bachelor'sThree
Completed vocational or trade welding classesFour
High school diploma or equivalentFive
Eighth gradeNine
Below eighth gradeTwelve

Candidates must also pass a vision test set by AWS. Once earned, the certification covers a nine-year span with interim renewals at the third and sixth years. More detail is in the CWI requirements guide; AWS keeps its exam and seminar charges current on aws.org, and the budget planning article helps you add the trip to a Part B site.

faq.q: Is there a CWI Part B exam site in Kansas City?
faq.a: Not on the AWS list as of November 2026. Tulsa is the nearest listed site for most of the metro, with Dallas, Denver, Chicago and Indianapolis as alternatives. Check aws.org for current dates.

faq.q: Where can I take Parts A and C near Kansas City?
faq.a: Prometric runs them in supervised centers around the country. Schedule a seat once AWS has issued the eligibility code in your confirmation letter.

faq.q: Does experience in Kansas count the same as experience in Missouri?
faq.a: Yes. The CWI is a national AWS certification, and AWS judges welding-related experience on what you did, not which state you did it in.

faq.q: Is a CWI useful for source inspection at vendor shops?
faq.a: Very often. Owners and engineering firms commonly require a CWI for the welding portion of vendor surveillance, alongside other qualifications the purchase order may name.

faq.q: Which Part C code fits pipeline work in Kansas and Missouri?
faq.a: API 1104, the pipeline welding standard. AWS offers its 22nd edition for Part C.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a training center in Kansas City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis works from Houston and Hyderabad. Kansas City learners prepare remotely, unless their company brings the six days onto its own premises.

faq.q: Can a Kansas City fabricator run the six days in house?
faq.a: Yes. A shop can book all six days on its own floor for several staff, and the practical exercises then use its production welds and its gauges. Request a quote.

faq.q: Does the course certify me as a welding inspector?
faq.a: No. AWS grants the CWI after you meet its eligibility rules, pass its vision test and score at least 72 percent on each exam part. Atlantis is not approved or endorsed by AWS.

faq.q: Does a JCCC or MCC welding program shorten the experience requirement?
faq.a: It can. AWS gives credit for college and vocational welding study, which reduces the experience it asks of a high school graduate. How a given program is classed is AWS's decision.

faq.q: Which AWS section covers Kansas City?
faq.a: The AWS Kansas City Section in District 16. AWS also lists a Kansas Section in the same district.
